body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Four camp talks about Lucan's personal story, the Thread of Slaughter. The companion is LUCAN HOUNDSTOOTH (call them Lucan in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE FIXED FACTS (the beats in the game's journal; the talks tell these, in Lucan's own words, and go no further than they do).
- Lucan's Thread: Lucan's Slaughter. What Lucan wants: Hunt the worst things in the dark woods, and stay the hunter.
- The Connection already happened in Wickermoor, with Hilda Brom, the huntress. The journal says: "Hilda Brom read Lucan's tracks in the Round, and some of what she read was not about wolves."
- The Discovery, "The Hound's Trail", happens in the Fields of the Crow (Foxwillow's cornfields). The journal's line for it: "In the Fields of the Crow Lucan followed his hound to a kill he had not made, and looked at the hound for a long time."
- The Confrontation, "The Hunter in the Wood", happens in Hartsblight (the forest). The journal's line for it: "In Hartsblight Lucan met the beast he is becoming, and chose which of them walks out."
Each talk is had at camp AFTER its chapter is over, so Lucan looks back on what happened. You may name the Fields of the Crow (Foxwillow's cornfields) in the Discovery and Hartsblight (the forest) in the Confrontation and no other place. Do not describe fights, bosses or villains; Lucan speaks of what was found, felt or chosen.

THE INCITEMENT AS IT PLAYED (for the first talk). Lucan sometimes misses this scene because Lucan is not with the party when it plays in the Trophy Room of the Crooked House. Then Lucan goes back alone, and at camp tells the party what was found. These are the facts of the scene; do not change them, you may add small sensory detail:
[slaughter_start]
  NARRATOR: Cedar and arsenic hang in the cold hearth air where glass-eyed beasts stand stiff around a brown bear on a plinth. Lucan opens his journal, then freezes as a boot-sized stuffed Pomeranian turns its head.
  LUCAN: Pay no mind to the cheddar, friends. Dreadfang has scented a prime specimen in that crow, and I give the taxidermist four out of ten for the beak.
  NARRATOR: The small ghost dog pads out from behind Lucan's boots and slips into the mount like a hand into a glove. It points its nose at a stuffed black crow high on a shelf, whose feathers smell of burnt straw, then yips at a crumb of cheddar on the bear's plinth.
  LUCAN: H-hush now, Barnaby, a hound of the elder woods does not solicit dairy while on duty, even if the provisioning in this manor is under three out of ten.
  the party can say: What's your hound pointing at, Lucan?
  the party can say: Did your omen of death just beg for cheese?
  the party can say: Leave the mounts. We've a house to clear.
[slaughter_shared]
  NARRATOR: Lucan steadies his pencil against his leather cuff and taps the tip toward the high shelf, where the black feathers smell of scorched straw.
  LUCAN: Observe the singed primaries on that corvid, if you please, for no respectable bird carries burnt straw into a parlour without foul husbandry afoot.
[slaughter_bristled]
  NARRATOR: Lucan tugs his long collar up over his ears and scratches the small stuffed dog behind one stiff ear with a gloved thumb.
  LUCAN: W-well, a phantom mastiff requires substantial tallow to maintain his bulk in this damp climate, and I find your tone toward my tracker frankly dreadful.
[slaughter_alone]
  NARRATOR: Lucan sketches the black crow in his field journal with a quick lead stroke, snappin' the cover shut before the little dog can yip again.
  LUCAN: Quite right, let us press onward in good order, though I have entered that bird at two out of ten for parlour hygiene.

THE TALKS. Write these four talks, in this order, with these keys.

TALK incitement. Lucan tells the party about the Trophy Room of the Crooked House as one short story at the fire. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 or 4 SAY rows (the story, in their own words, ending on a plain statement of how it left them). TWO options only: OPTION 1 asks to hear more or says something that shares the moment; OPTION 2 is the quiet way on, leaving Lucan to it. Two replies of 1 NARRATOR row (optional) and 1 or 2 SAY rows. No REASON rows in this talk.

TALK discovery. Lucan has come back from the Fields of the Crow (Foxwillow's cornfields) with the Discovery, and wants to tell it. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row to open the scene at the fire, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row is allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Lucan's own words and end on the turn: how it sits with them, with one thing left unsaid (never the dark secret: no names, deeds or places from the note's dark-secret section). Three options: OPTION 1 asks Lucan to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Lucan would want to hear, meeting Lucan on Lucan's own terms; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, civil but brisk, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply (3) must still leave the Discovery told.

TALK confrontation_wait. Lucan is at their lowest regard for the party (Strained), and has the Confrontation to tell about Hartsblight (the forest) but is holding it back until things are mended. This talk is short. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row and 3 or 4 SAY rows: Lucan says there is something to say about it and it will keep, and says, in Lucan's own voice, what matters to Lucan and that the party's way has drifted from it (do not claim any specific deed the party did). Three options: OPTION 1 listens and owns it (the way to mend); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing and gives Lucan room (its option text is plain words such as "Say nothing. Stay by the fire."; this reply has NO REASON row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows. Nothing is lost for good: even the cold reply leaves the door open.

TALK confrontation. Lucan's story comes to a head. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 7 to 9 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Lucan's own words: the heart of their act-three story, plain and a little raw, never grand; Lucan may say that something from before has found them, but must NOT name or describe the person, the act or the event behind the dark secret (no names, deeds, places or objects from the note's dark-secret section, or from its Climax and Catharsis sections): say only what it was like to stand one's ground against it; end on the turn and a question or a long silence. Three options: OPTION 1 asks Lucan to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Lucan needs to hear; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply must still leave the Confrontation told.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: incitement, discovery, confrontation_wait, confrontation.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/lucan_houndstooth-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for LUCAN HOUNDSTOOTH (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Lucan likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/lucan_houndstooth-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Lucan, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK incitement
NARRATOR: Lucan sits close to the coals, rubbin' a smear of cedar dust from his cuff while the spectral hound curls tight around his boots.
SAY: I took the liberty of inspecting the Trophy Room in that crooked manor alone, friends, though the arsenic and dry rot merited a dismal grade.
SAY: Dreadfang stepped directly into the mount of a boot-sized Pomeranian to point at a stuffed crow high on the shelf.
SAY: The bird's feathers reeked of burnt straw, and the hound begged for a crumb of cheddar on the bear's plinth before I called him off.
SAY: We have a quarry in the brush that smells of scorched harvest, and my hound is already shrinking from its shadow.
OPTION 1: What did you make of the burnt straw on that crow?
OPTION 2: Keep your notes dry. We move at first light.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan taps his brass pencil against his leather journal, his ears twitching toward the dark beyond the firelight.
SAY: No natural corvid brings field-ash into a parlour, if you please, unless something wicked is wearing the flock like a hunting coat.
SAY: I have entered the spoor in my ledger, and we shall follow the smoke when you give the word.
REPLY 2
SAY: Quite right, friends, a huntsman does not clutter the camp with speculation when the trail is already warm.
SAY: I shall keep the watch until the embers settle, if you please.
TALK discovery
NARRATOR: Lucan stares into the flames with his field journal shut across his knee, while a larger, heavier shadow breathes beside his stool.
SAY: Out in the Fields of the Crow, Dreadfang broke from my heel and took a trail through the dry stalks that I had not called.
SAY: I followed his spoor to a fresh kill in the dirt that neither my rifle nor his spectral jaws had made.
SAY: Whatever tore that quarry apart left no honest print in the mud, only a cold wake that made the hair along my spine stand stiff.
NARRATOR: He reaches down to lay his gloved palm between the ghost hound's shoulder blades, where the pale fur rises thick and coarse.
SAY: Dreadfang stood over those remains and drank the rising dark of it until his ribs swelled to the size of a timber wolf.
SAY: He did not look for a crust in my pocket, friends, and I looked at him for a very long time in that corn.
SAY: Good heavens, I came into this valley to hunt the worst things in the brush, yet my own tracker is growing into a specimen I scarcely recognise.
SAY: It is not the first time I have stood over a kill that was not mine and let the dark dress me larger than I am.
OPTION 1: What do you see when you look at him now?
OPTION 2: Whatever he grows into, you are still the huntsman holding the lead.
OPTION 3: So long as he tracks true, we use him. Get some sleep.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan clears his throat softly, his thumb tracing the brass clasp of his closed book.
SAY: I see a very small dog from my grandfather's kennels trying so terribly hard to look fierce that he is forgetting how to wag.
SAY: If we are not careful on the next stalk, I fear neither of us will remember the way back to the hearth.
REASON: You asked what I saw in my hound after the Fields of the Crow.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: The yellow at the rim of Lucan's eyes eases as he gives a slow, grateful bow of his head.
SAY: That is most generously spoken, friends, for a gentleman of the hunt is nothing without the discipline of his pack.
SAY: Hush now, the dark has teeth in these pastures, so we shall keep our posture clean and our lanterns high.
REASON: You reminded me that I still hold the lead after the Fields of the Crow.
REPLY 3
SAY: By your leave, we shall keep the relationship strictly professional and set our boots to the next spoor.
SAY: Sleep well by the embers, friends, while Dreadfang and I take the perimeter.
REASON: You told me to get some sleep after I spoke of the Fields of the Crow.
TALK confrontation_wait
NARRATOR: Lucan stands a pace back from the fire's circle, buttonin' his crimson coat to the throat with stiff, neat fingers.
SAY: There is a matter from the deep brush of Hartsblight that belongs in the company ledger, friends, though the ink will keep for a fairer evening.
SAY: A gentleman of the hunt walks the wood with patience, a quiet heel, and a decent regard for the small creatures under his boots.
SAY: Of late our stride has grown noisy and rough, and I cannot lay a delicate specimen on the table while our manners are so badly frayed.
OPTION 1: You're right. We've been careless in the brush, and we'll mend it.
OPTION 2: Save the lecture on manners. Keep your Hartsblight story to yourself.
OPTION 3: Say nothing. Stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan lets his hand fall from his lapel and gives a measured nod toward the kettle.
SAY: That is the proper spirit for the field, if you please, and when our pace settles I shall gladly share what met me under those boughs.
REASON: You owned our rough stride and promised to mend it.
REPLY 2
SAY: As you wish, friends, I shall keep my counsel and my rifle clean until the company has use for a scholar of the spoor.
REASON: You told me to save my lecture and keep Hartsblight to myself.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Lucan watches the sparks lift into the pines for a moment, then tips his tricorn and steps back to his bedroll.
SAY: May the night stay quiet around your blankets, friends.
TALK confrontation
NARRATOR: Lucan sits with his tricorn off and his sleeves rolled to the elbow, turnin' a cold cartridge between his thumb and forefinger.
SAY: In the rot of Hartsblight, where the moss hangs heavy on the stone, Dreadfang cornered a shadow that smelled of old fog and wet wool.
SAY: When the hound lifted his head from the brush, he was standing as tall as my chest and wearing my own wolfen face.
SAY: Every yellow terror I ever hid behind a polite grade and a crimson coat was staring back at me through his eyes.
NARRATOR: The ghost hound rests his heavy chin across Lucan's boot, and the wolf-man does not pull his foot away.
SAY: A beast like that wants you to snarl and bluff, friends, or else bolt into the gorse and let another bear the teeth.
SAY: For the first time since I left Edwardia, I did not check my ledger or reach for a grand title to hide the shaking in my knees.
SAY: I told the brute in the mirror that he was only a frightened creature in an oversized pelt, and I chose which of us was walking out of the trees.
SAY: The hunter walked out, if you please, though without the swagger, I wonder if the company finds me a rather smaller specimen by the fire.
OPTION 1: Tell us what it took to stand your ground in those trees.
OPTION 2: A hunter who doesn't need to bluff is the one we want beside us.
OPTION 3: You walked out of Hartsblight whole. That's enough for tonight.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Lucan sets the cartridge down on his knee, his voice drop-hushed and steady over the crackle of the pine.
SAY: It took admitting to the dark that my hands have never been as steady as my calligraphy, and that the dog was only trying to shield me.
SAY: Once a man stops lying to his own hound, the brush loses half its teeth.
REASON: You asked what it took to stand my ground in Hartsblight.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Lucan's ears lift, and a genuine, quiet warmth softens the long line of his jaw.
SAY: Prime specimen of comradeship, friends, and I would not trade this fireside for the finest hall in Edwardia.
SAY: Come what may on the trail ahead, my rifle and my hound are yours without reserve.
REASON: You said a hunter who does not bluff is who you want beside you.
REPLY 3
SAY: Quite so, friends, the wood is behind us and the watch is set in good order.
SAY: Take your rest while the coals hold, if you please.
REASON: You said walking out of Hartsblight whole was enough for tonight.
